## Deny always wins
`deny` disallows access and takes precedence regardless of any other capabilities defined for the path, including `sudo`. When the same pattern appears in two policies, the union of capabilities contains `deny`, which cancels the result.
- Use it to carve an exception out of a broad grant, such as a global `secret/*` policy with `deny` on a specific sensitive path.
- A separate "block" policy is a convenient way to remove access from selected users without editing a shared policy.
- Because a token's policy list is fixed, removing a deny means editing the policy or getting a new token.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Grant first:** there is no grants-before-denials order; deny wins on the path no matter which policy lists it.
- ✓ **B. Deny precedence (correct):** any `deny` on the matched pattern overrides all grants for it, so the read fails.
- ✗ **C. Sudo rescue:** `sudo` does not override deny, which is explicitly stronger.
- ✗ **D. Group-only:** deny applies the same way no matter how a policy was attached to the token.

## Key idea
Deny overrides every other capability on the same path.
Q009803:
## Translating a requirement into stanzas
Break the requirement into operations, then map each to a v2 path and capability.
- "Read every secret" is a GET on `secret/data/payroll/...`, so `read` on `secret/data/payroll/*`.
- "List its key names" is a LIST on `secret/metadata/payroll/...`, so `list` on `secret/metadata/payroll/*`.
- "Must not write" means no `create`, `update`, `patch` or `delete` anywhere.
Because deny is the default, nothing else is needed.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. v1 style path:** `secret/payroll/*` matches nothing on a KV v2 mount, so neither read nor list would ever apply.
- ✗ **B. Metadata delete:** delete permanently removes keys, a write-type action that auditors must not have.
- ✗ **C. Write access:** create and update on the data path would let auditors write, which is forbidden.
- ✓ **D. Metadata list (correct):** this grants key enumeration under the payroll prefix and nothing more.
- ✓ **E. Data read (correct):** this grants the GET on every secret value below the payroll prefix.

## Key idea
Translate each required operation to its KV v2 path and capability, and grant nothing beyond them.
Q009804:
## Priority between different patterns
Both paths match `secret/data/billing/prod`. Their first wildcard appears in the same position (right after `secret/data/`), so the next rule applies: a path ending in `*` has lower priority than one that does not.
- `secret/data/+/prod` ends in a literal and wins.
- Its capability list is `deny`, so the read fails.
- `secret/data/billing/dev` still matches only the glob, so it stays readable.
When results seem surprising, `vault token capabilities <token> <path>` shows what Vault computes.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Plus always wins:** there is no rule that `+` outranks `*` unconditionally; the position of the first wildcard and the ending are compared.
- ✓ **B. Ends-in-glob rule (correct):** the stanza ending in `*` is lower priority, so the deny stanza decides and the request fails.
- ✗ **C. Broader wins:** priority favors the more specific match, not the one covering more paths.
- ✗ **D. Union across patterns:** union is for identical patterns; different ones are resolved by priority.

## Key idea
For different patterns, the more specific one wins, and a pattern ending in `*` ranks below one that does not.
Q009805:
## Policies on child tokens
Tokens receive their policies at creation. For explicit token creation, the policies that may be specified are normally those in the parent's own token policies, so a token cannot hand out more power than it has. Root tokens can assign any policy.
- The parent here holds `default` and `dev-reader`, so it could create a child with either or both.
- `admin` is outside its set, so the request is refused rather than trimmed.
- The child's policy list cannot be changed later; wrong grants mean revoking the token and creating a new one.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Checked later:** the restriction is enforced when the token is created, not postponed to use time.
- ✗ **B. Silent drop:** Vault refuses the request, which avoids a child that differs from what was asked for.
- ✓ **C. Subset rule (correct):** a non-root parent can only delegate policies it already holds, so requesting `admin` fails.
- ✗ **D. Sudo on policy path:** `sys/policy/admin` is the policy management path and has nothing to do with attaching policies to tokens.

## Key idea
A non-root token can give a child only the policies it holds, whereas a root token may assign any.
Q009806:
## Templated policies
Policy `path` values may contain variables that Vault replaces with identity information of the requesting token, so one policy serves everyone.
- `{{identity.entity.id}}`, `{{identity.entity.name}}`, `{{identity.entity.metadata.<key>}}`
- `{{identity.entity.aliases.<mount accessor>.name}}` and related alias fields
- `{{identity.groups.ids.<id>.name}}` and `{{identity.groups.names.<name>}}` fields
Use IDs where possible: an ID is unique to the user, while names can change and be reused, so an ID keeps the policy pointing at the intended entity.
A typical pair of stanzas gives the owner `read`/`create`/`update`/`delete` on `secret/data/{{identity.entity.id}}/*` and `list` on `secret/metadata/{{identity.entity.id}}/*`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Name template:** it also isolates users, but names can change and be reused, so the folder could pass to a different person; the requirement says it must follow the user.
- ✗ **B. Whole prefix:** this grants all folders to all users, which is the opposite of private.
- ✗ **C. Single-segment wildcard:** this matches every user's folder, so everyone can touch everyone else's data.
- ✓ **D. Entity ID template (correct):** it renders to a unique, stable identifier, so each user reaches only their own folder even after a rename.

## Key idea
Templated policies inject identity values into paths; prefer entity or group IDs over names.
Q009807:
## Rendering rules for templates
Vault substitutes identity values before matching the path. Substituted values are treated as literal text and cannot introduce wildcards.
- Using `+` or `*` in the rendered output results in permission denied.
- A server setting, `deny_slash_in_templated_paths`, controls whether a rendered value that contains `/` is also denied.
This prevents a user who controls a piece of metadata from widening their own access.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Wildcard in output (correct):** rendered wildcards are rejected, so the request returns permission denied.
- ✗ **B. List only:** there is no special wildcard handling for list requests in template output.
- ✗ **C. Wildcard expansion:** that would let metadata values widen access, which Vault explicitly prevents.
- ✗ **D. Fallback:** Vault does not fall back to a policy without the template; the request is simply denied.

## Key idea
Wildcards (`+` or `*`) in a rendered template value cause permission denied.
Q009808:
## Managing policies from the CLI
`vault policy` has four subcommands: `write` (upload a named policy), `read` (print its contents), `list` (list installed policies) and `delete` (remove one by name). `vault policy fmt` formats a local file.
- `vault policy write NAME PATH` loads the file at PATH; when PATH is `-` the policy is read from standard input.
- Writing with an existing name replaces that policy, and the change applies to every token that uses it from its next request.
- The API equivalent is a POST with a `policy` parameter to `/sys/policy/NAME`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Upload subcommand:** upload is not a `vault policy` subcommand; the name used is `write`.
- ✓ **B. Write with dash (correct):** `vault policy write` accepts `-` as the path, which reads the policy from standard input.
- ✗ **C. Create subcommand:** there is no `create` subcommand, and without a path or `-` the command would not know where the policy comes from.
- ✗ **D. Raw write:** the legacy endpoint expects a `policy` parameter containing the rules, and there is no `file` parameter that reads a local file.

## Key idea
`vault policy write NAME PATH` uploads a policy, and `-` as the path reads it from standard input.
Q009809:
## Inspecting policies
- `vault policy list` lists the installed policies, including the built-in `default` and `root`.
- `vault policy read NAME` prints the contents of one policy; with `-format` you can get json or yaml. It returns an error if the policy does not exist.
- `vault policy fmt PATH` rewrites a local file in canonical format; it does not talk to the server's stored policy.
- `vault policy delete NAME` removes a policy, and tokens that reference it are affected immediately. The `default` and `root` policies cannot be deleted.
Equivalent API calls: GET `/sys/policy` and GET `/sys/policy/NAME`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Show:** this is not a `vault policy` subcommand; the supported ones are write, read, list, delete and fmt.
- ✗ **B. Format:** it reformats a local file and does not print anything stored on the server.
- ✗ **C. Delete:** it removes the policy, which is destructive and shows no rules.
- ✓ **D. Read (correct):** it prints the rules and metadata of the named policy.
- ✓ **E. List (correct):** it enumerates the installed policy names.

## Key idea
Use `vault policy list` for names and `vault policy read NAME` for rules.
Q009810:
## Finding the policy a command needs
Adding `-output-policy` to a CLI command prints the HCL policy that the request would require instead of performing it. For `vault kv get -mount=secret -output-policy app/db` on KV v2 it prints a stanza for `secret/data/app/db` with `read`.
- It is the quickest way to learn the `data/` and `metadata/` paths a command uses.
- `vault token capabilities [TOKEN] PATH` is for checking what an existing token may do on a path (it returns `root` for a root token).
- `vault policy fmt` only reformats a file.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Format:** `fmt` only rewrites an existing file into canonical style and cannot infer missing rules.
- ✗ **B. Copy default:** the default policy holds basics such as token self-lookup; it says nothing about the target secret, and a `secret/*` grant would be too broad and wrong for v2.
- ✓ **C. Output policy flag (correct):** the flag prints the required policy without running the request, giving the exact path and capability.
- ✗ **D. Root capabilities:** a root token reports root capability for every path, so the output reveals nothing about the minimum policy.

## Key idea
Add `-output-policy` to a CLI command to print the policy that command needs.
Q009811:
## Built-in policies
Vault ships two policies.
- `default`: cannot be removed. It is attached to all tokens unless excluded when the token is created (for example `-no-default-policy` on `vault token create`, or `no_default_policy` in the API). It holds basics such as looking up the token itself and using its cubbyhole. Its content can be edited, and Vault never overwrites your changes; to track upstream, copy the content from an up-to-date dev server.
- `root`: cannot be modified or removed. Any token with it can do anything, so root tokens should be revoked after the initial setup and replaced by more strictly controlled access.
View the default policy with `vault read sys/policy/default` or `vault policy read default`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Default attach (correct):** the policy is attached by default and can be omitted at creation time using `-no-default-policy`.
- ✗ **B. Editable root:** the `root` policy cannot be modified or removed; narrower access needs another policy.
- ✗ **C. Deletable:** `default` is a built-in policy that cannot be removed, even by root.
- ✗ **D. Overwritten on upgrade:** Vault does not prescribe the contents and never overwrites your modifications.

## Key idea
`default` is on every token unless excluded and cannot be deleted, while `root` can be neither changed nor removed.
Q009812:
## Choosing an engine by what the consumer needs
Start from the question "who creates the secret?" If a person or system creates it and Vault only stores it, use a storage engine such as KV. If the target system can have credentials created on demand, use an engine that generates them.
## The database secrets engine
The database secrets engine connects to a database through a plugin using a privileged "root" user configured for Vault. Roles contain the SQL statements that create a user. Each read of a creds path produces a new username and password with a lease, and Vault revokes the user when the lease ends.
- Setup: `vault secrets enable database`, then configure the connection and a role.
- Result: every instance has distinct credentials, so audit logs point to one instance.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. KV version 2:** it stores values somebody else has already created. A nightly job would create shared or long-lived passwords by hand, and nothing makes them disappear after a few hours.
- ✗ **B. Cubbyhole:** it is a private store tied to one token. It keeps whatever a client writes and does not create database users or expire them on its own schedule.
- ✗ **C. Transit:** it encrypts and decrypts data for applications and does not create database accounts, so a password kept in the database would still be a static credential.
- ✓ **D. Database secrets engine (correct):** it generates a unique database user per request from the role's statements and removes the user when the lease expires, which is exactly the per-instance, self-expiring requirement.

## Key idea
When the target system can mint accounts on demand, use a dynamic engine like database so each consumer gets unique, expiring credentials.
Q009813:
## Dynamic cloud credentials
The AWS secrets engine generates AWS credentials from IAM policies defined in a Vault role. The credentials are time-based and are revoked when the Vault lease expires.
Four credential types exist:
- `iam_user`: Vault creates an IAM user for each lease and deletes it at expiry.
- `assumed_role`, `federation_token`, `session_token`: Vault calls STS and returns an access key, secret key and session token.
The pipeline authenticates to Vault with its own auth method, so no AWS secret needs to live in the CI system.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. AWS secrets engine (correct):** roles map to IAM policies or STS calls, so each pipeline run receives fresh keys that Vault removes at lease expiry. Nothing long-lived has to be stored in CI.
- ✗ **B. KV version 1:** a stored access key is exactly the long-lived static credential the team wants to avoid; reading it repeatedly does not make it short-lived.
- ✗ **C. Identity:** it keeps entities and aliases inside Vault to unify logins, and does not create or map IAM users in AWS.
- ✗ **D. PKI:** it issues X.509 certificates, and AWS API calls are authorized with access keys or STS sessions rather than a client certificate from Vault.

## Key idea
The AWS secrets engine turns an IAM policy into short-lived access keys, so CI never stores long-term AWS credentials.
Q009814:
## Certificates as dynamic secrets
The PKI secrets engine generates dynamic X.509 certificates. Services obtain certificates without generating a key and CSR, submitting it to a certificate authority and waiting for approval; Vault authentication and policies replace the manual verification.
Keeping TTLs short means revocation is rarely needed, CRLs stay small, and each running instance can hold its own certificate.
- Roles define allowed domains and TTLs.
- Certificates can be held in memory and discarded at shutdown.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Transit:** it performs cryptographic operations on data such as encrypt, sign and HMAC. It does not act as a certificate authority that issues X.509 certificates.
- ✗ **B. KV version 2:** storing certificates only holds files someone else produced, so the manual issuance process stays in place and nothing is generated on demand.
- ✓ **C. PKI (correct):** it works as a certificate authority and issues a certificate on request, constrained by role settings, which removes the manual CSR process for every microservice.
- ✗ **D. SSH:** its signed certificates are SSH certificates for logging in to machines, a different format from the X.509 certificates TLS requires.

## Key idea
PKI makes certificate issuance an API call, ideally with short TTLs.
Q009815:
## SSH secrets engine modes
The SSH secrets engine manages access to machines over the SSH protocol. It provides two documented modes:
- Signed SSH certificates: Vault signs a public key presented by the client, and servers trust the Vault CA.
- One-time SSH passwords: Vault issues a password valid for one login, checked by a helper on the host.
The dynamic keys mode was deprecated in Vault 1.12 and removed in 1.13, so it is not a choice for Vault 1.19.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Dynamic keys:** that mode was removed in Vault 1.13 and is not available in current versions.
- ✓ **B. Certificates and one-time passwords (correct):** those are the two current modes, and dynamic keys no longer exist after Vault 1.13, so any design must use one of the first two.
- ✗ **C. Stored private keys:** the engine does not hold private keys for engineers to retrieve; it signs public keys or issues one-time credentials.
- ✗ **D. Passwords only:** signed SSH certificates are a mode of the SSH engine itself; PKI produces X.509 certificates, not SSH certificates.

## Key idea
SSH engine means signed certificates or one-time passwords, with no permanent keys to distribute.
Q009816:
## KV is for static secrets that you supply
The KV secrets engine stores arbitrary key-value data that you provide. It has two modes.
- Version 1 stores only the latest value; an update overwrites the old one and it is not recoverable. It uses less storage and has fewer storage calls.
- Version 2 retains a configurable number of versions (default 10), supports check-and-set to avoid unintended overwrite, and lets deleted versions be restored.
A third-party API key is a static secret that Vault cannot create, which is a KV use case.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cubbyhole:** values are replaced on write and are destroyed with the token, so they offer neither history nor durable storage for the team.
- ✗ **B. KV version 1:** updates overwrite the old value and it cannot be recovered. The saving in storage is the trade-off for no history.
- ✓ **C. KV version 2 (correct):** versions let an operator read an earlier value or roll back after a mistaken write.
- ✗ **D. Database engine:** it generates database credentials and is not a general store for third-party keys or their earlier values.

## Key idea
Pick KV version 2 for static secrets that need history and recovery.
Q009817:
## Store, generate or encrypt
Secrets engines are grouped by function: some store and read data, some generate dynamic credentials, some provide encryption and similar operations.
- Storing: KV (both versions) and cubbyhole return what a client wrote.
- Generating: database, AWS, PKI and SSH produce credentials, certificates or signed keys on request.
A quick test is whether you can read a value from the engine that you never wrote there.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cubbyhole:** it stores only what a client writes in the token's private space, and renewing a lease does not generate anything.
- ✗ **B. KV version 1:** it returns the last value written. Listing shows key names and does not create values.
- ✗ **C. KV version 2:** it returns the data an operator wrote; versioning keeps history and never invents values.
- ✓ **D. PKI (correct):** issuing a certificate generates a key pair and certificate from the role's constraints.
- ✓ **E. Database (correct):** reading a creds path executes the role's creation statements and returns a new user.

## Key idea
Dynamic engines create the secret; storage engines only return what you wrote.
Q009818:
## Encryption as a service
The transit secrets engine handles cryptographic functions on data in transit. Vault does not store the data sent to it. Applications keep the ciphertext in their own primary data store, and the burden of correct encryption moves from developers to Vault operators.
Besides encrypt and decrypt, transit can sign and verify data, generate hashes and HMACs, and return random bytes. Details of rotation and rewrap are a separate topic.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Vault stores records:** transit does not store the data sent to it; storing is the job of the application's database or a KV engine.
- ✓ **B. Send plaintext, store ciphertext (correct):** Vault performs the cryptography with a key that never leaves it, and the data itself remains in MySQL.
- ✗ **C. Key returned to the app:** the main benefit of transit is that the named key stays inside Vault, so developers never handle it.
- ✗ **D. Lease on the key for the database engine:** transit has no such lease and the database engine produces credentials, not encryption of table contents.

## Key idea
Transit encrypts data for applications while the ciphertext stays in their own store and the key stays in Vault.
Q009819:
## Transit at purpose level
Transit is cryptography as a service. For this exam you should know what it is for, and when to prefer it over KV or database.
- Encrypt and decrypt application data without Vault storing it.
- Sign and verify, hash, HMAC, random bytes.
- Key derivation, including optional convergent encryption, and data key generation.
Choose KV when Vault should hold the secret itself; choose transit when the data belongs in another system.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Broader cryptographic functions (correct):** signing, verification, hashing, HMACs and random bytes are documented functions of transit besides encryption.
- ✗ **B. Replaces barrier encryption:** the barrier protects everything Vault writes to storage, and transit is a separate service for client data.
- ✗ **C. Stores the data:** transit does not store the data sent to it; KV is the engine for storing data in Vault.
- ✗ **D. Dynamic database logins:** producing logins is the database engine's role, and transit has no connection to databases.

## Key idea
Transit is a general cryptography service and not a store.
Q009820:
## Static versus dynamic
- Static secrets are values placed in Vault, as in KV. They are read as many times as needed and remain until someone updates or deletes them. Anyone with read access sees the same value.
- Dynamic secrets do not exist until a client asks. Vault generates the credential on demand (database, AWS, and so on) and attaches a lease so it expires and can be revoked.
Because each request produces a distinct credential, dynamic secrets support per-client auditing and limit blast radius.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Access path limits:** every secret type can be accessed through the CLI, API and UI.
- ✗ **B. Reversed roles:** operators supply static secrets, while Vault itself generates dynamic ones.
- ✗ **C. No expiry for dynamic:** dynamic secrets carry leases that expire, and static KV values do not depend on the reader's token lifetime.
- ✓ **D. Generated with a lease vs stored (correct):** that is the defining contrast; dynamic values come from a request, expire and can be revoked, and static values persist until changed.

## Key idea
Dynamic means generated on request with a lease; static means stored until changed.
Q009821:
## Static roles in the database engine
Static roles are a one-to-one mapping between a Vault role and an existing database username. Vault stores the password and rotates it based on a period or schedule. Clients receive the current password for the user.
- Trade-off: access is not unique per client, and anyone allowed to read the role can use the same database account.
- Never assign the root credentials Vault uses in `config/` to a static role; rotating them would break the other roles.
Dynamic roles are the better choice when an application can request fresh credentials.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Database static role (correct):** the account stays the same and Vault handles password rotation on a controlled schedule, which suits an application tied to one username.
- ✗ **B. Cubbyhole:** values change only when a client writes them, and renewing the token does not touch the contents.
- ✗ **C. Dynamic role:** every request creates a new user, which suits applications that can fetch credentials again but not one tied to a fixed account.
- ✗ **D. KV version 1:** KV stores whatever is written and never rotates values or has any logic tied to reads.

## Key idea
Static roles keep a fixed database user but have Vault rotate its password.
Q009822:
## Choosing static or dynamic
Dynamic secrets require a target system Vault can reach and control. When the value originates elsewhere, or is configuration rather than a credential, a static store is the right tool.
- Static: vendor-issued keys, shared configuration, values with no API to mint them.
- Dynamic: database users, cloud keys, per-instance certificates, anything that benefits from expiry.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Ten-minute AWS credential:** the AWS secrets engine can generate this with an expiry that matches the job.
- ✓ **B. Vendor license key (correct):** Vault cannot create it, so an operator stores it in KV and updates it when the vendor changes it.
- ✗ **C. Per-pod database login:** the database engine can create a unique user for each pod.
- ✗ **D. Per-instance certificate:** PKI can issue a new certificate per instance with a short TTL, so this is the dynamic case.
- ✓ **E. Configuration string (correct):** it is an edited value read by several applications and has no account or certificate for Vault to generate.

## Key idea
If Vault cannot mint the value, it is a static secret for KV.
Q009823:
## What a secrets engine is
Secrets engines are enabled at a path. When a request arrives, the router sends anything under that prefix to the engine, which defines its own paths and properties. To users they act like a virtual filesystem with read, write and delete operations.
- Some engines store data (KV), some generate credentials (database, AWS), some encrypt (transit), and others produce certificates (PKI).
- Auth methods, audit devices and the seal are separate components.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Audit device:** logging requests and responses is done by audit devices.
- ✗ **B. Seal and key storage:** protecting keys and unsealing belong to the seal mechanism, not to engines.
- ✓ **C. Mounted component that stores, generates or encrypts (correct):** the router sends requests under the mount's prefix to the engine, which handles them with its own API.
- ✗ **D. Auth method:** verifying identity and issuing tokens is what auth methods do, mounted under `auth/`.

## Key idea
A secrets engine is a path-mounted component that stores, generates or encrypts data.
Q009824:
## Mount points cannot overlap
Mount points must not conflict. You cannot create a mount that is prefixed by an existing one, and you cannot create a mount whose name is a prefix of an existing one.
- `foo/bar` and `foo/baz` can coexist.
- `foo` and `foo/baz` cannot.
Each engine is isolated to its own path, so mounts never share data.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Prefix conflict (correct):** `apps/team1` is under the existing `apps/` mount, so Vault rejects it; sibling mounts below a common prefix that is not itself a mount are fine.
- ✗ **B. Depends on type:** the rule applies to every pair of mounts, regardless of type.
- ✗ **C. Automatic move:** enabling never relocates an engine; moving is a separate `vault secrets move` operation that revokes leases.
- ✗ **D. Shared data:** each engine is isolated and has its own storage prefix, so it never shares data with another.

## Key idea
Mounts may be siblings but never a prefix of one another.
Q009825:
## Secrets engine lifecycle
An engine can be enabled, disabled, moved and tuned.
- Move: changes the path of an existing engine. All secrets are revoked, since leases are tied to the path where they were created, but the stored configuration persists.
- Tune: changes global settings such as TTLs.
Plan moves in a maintenance window because clients holding credentials lose them.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Leases carried over:** they cannot survive, because they are tied to the old path.
- ✗ **B. Alias to old path:** Vault has no alias for mounts; the engine is relocated.
- ✗ **C. Delete and recreate:** the configuration persists through a move, which is the point of the command.
- ✓ **D. Configuration kept, secrets revoked (correct):** leases belong to the original path, so the move revokes them while connection settings and roles stay.

## Key idea
Moving an engine keeps its configuration but revokes its secrets.
Q009826:
## Barrier view
When a secrets engine is enabled, Vault generates a random UUID that becomes the data root of that engine. Everything it writes is prefixed with it, and since storage has no relative access like `../`, an engine cannot reach beyond its folder. This works like a chroot, so even a malicious engine cannot read the data of other engines.
This is separate from policy checks that apply to API callers.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Separate nodes:** engines run inside the same Vault process and do not need separate nodes.
- ✓ **B. Barrier view with UUID prefix (correct):** the engine can only address its own folder in storage, which isolates engines from one another.
- ✗ **C. Enabling token's policy:** policies govern API callers, but internal storage access by engine code is limited by the barrier view.
- ✗ **D. Separate unseal keys:** Vault has one seal and unseal process for the whole barrier, not one per engine.

## Key idea
Engines see storage through a UUID-prefixed barrier view, like a chroot.
Q009827:
## Cubbyhole
Cubbyhole is private per-token storage. The lifetime of its data is tied to the token, so there is no TTL or refresh interval for the values, and the data is destroyed when the token expires. Writing a key replaces the old value.
It is enabled by default and cannot be disabled, moved or enabled again. Response wrapping builds on it: the wrapped response sits in the cubbyhole of a single-use token.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Versioned values:** cubbyhole replaces the old value on write and keeps no history.
- ✗ **B. Root can read others:** no token can access another token's cubbyhole, including privileged ones.
- ✓ **C. Per-token scope (correct):** each token only has access to its own cubbyhole, which is what makes it suitable for wrapping.
- ✗ **D. Survives the token:** the cubbyhole is destroyed with its token.
- ✓ **E. Always present (correct):** it is on by default and cannot be disabled, moved or enabled a second time.

## Key idea
Cubbyhole is private to one token and disappears with it.
Q009828:
## Response wrapping
Response wrapping lets Vault take the response it would have returned and place it in the cubbyhole of a new single-use token, returning that token instead. Wrapping is per request, triggered by a TTL in the `X-Vault-Wrap-TTL` header or `-wrap-ttl` on the CLI.
- The original response is serialized and stored in the new token's cubbyhole.
- The reply carries the token, its TTL, creation time and creation path.
- Unwrapping is done with `sys/wrapping/unwrap`, and works once.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Renewable read token:** the wrapping token is single-use and gives access only to the stored response.
- ✗ **B. Plaintext with short lease:** wrapping replaces the response with a token, so the secret is not on the wire.
- ✗ **C. Transit-encrypted copy:** wrapping does not involve transit or any key on the receiving machine.
- ✓ **D. Single-use token (correct):** the wrapping token only references the data, and a single unwrap returns the original response.

## Key idea
Wrapping swaps the secret for a single-use token that unwraps once.
Q009829:
## Validating wrapping tokens
A wrapping token can be unwrapped only once, so a failure suggests that another party got there first. Recommended validation:
- Alert if an expected token never arrives.
- Look up the token (`sys/wrapping/lookup`, unauthenticated for the holder); it shows creation time, creation path and TTL.
- Check that the creation path matches expectations, such as `pki/issue/...` for a certificate. Paths from `cubbyhole` or `sys/wrapping/wrap` are suspicious.
- Unwrap. A failure triggers investigation.
A failure does not prove interception, because a slow start can also let the TTL pass, but it must be investigated.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Inactive state:** wrapping tokens are usable immediately and need no renewal.
- ✗ **B. Policy for original path:** the token itself authorizes the unwrap; the holder needs no policy for the original path.
- ✓ **C. Possible earlier unwrap (correct):** single-use semantics mean a valid, unexpired token that fails to unwrap may have been used by someone else, which is the malfeasance detection that wrapping provides.
- ✗ **D. Lost data:** wrapped responses are stored in the token's cubbyhole, which is persisted, so loss is not the expected explanation.

## Key idea
A wrapping token that cannot be unwrapped before its TTL ends is a security signal.
Q009830:
## Where did it come from
The lookup operation on `sys/wrapping/lookup` returns the creation time, creation path and TTL of the wrapping token. It is unauthenticated for the holder so that validation is always allowed. If the path differs, the data may have been read and re-wrapped by an interceptor, especially if the path starts with `cubbyhole` or `sys/wrapping/wrap`.
Vault does not provide signed wrapping tokens, because validation is done against the server anyway.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Lookup and compare the creation path (correct):** it shows the API path of the original request without exposing the secret, and a mismatch reveals tampering.
- ✗ **B. Signature:** Vault does not currently provide signed response-wrapping tokens.
- ✗ **C. Read then re-wrap:** reading consumes the token and the new wrap would show a creation path of the rewrap, which hides the origin.
- ✗ **D. List the cubbyhole:** no token can access another token's cubbyhole, and lookup already provides the path.

## Key idea
Look up first and compare the creation path, then unwrap.
Q009831:
## What wrapping provides
Response wrapping performs three duties:
- Cover: the value on the wire is a reference to the secret, so logs do not see it.
- Malfeasance detection: only one party can unwrap, and a failed unwrap or lookup raises an alert.
- Limited exposure: the wrapping token has its own, often much shorter, TTL.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Inherited TTL:** the wrapping token has a separate lifetime chosen by the requester, often shorter.
- ✓ **B. Cover (correct):** the intermediate system and its logs see only the wrapping token.
- ✗ **C. Repeated unwrap:** wrapping tokens are single use, so a second unwrap attempt fails whatever time remains on the token TTL.
- ✗ **D. Re-generation:** the original serialized response is stored and returned as is.
- ✓ **E. Detect interception (correct):** a second unwrap fails, so a client holding a token that cannot be unwrapped has evidence of tampering.

## Key idea
Wrapping gives cover, tamper detection and a short exposure window.
Q009832:
## Why short-lived credentials
With dynamic secrets, services do not hardcode credentials. Because each service has unique credentials, auditing questionable access is easier: a SQL username can lead to one instance. Vault's revocation makes the users invalid soon after the lease ends.
- Smaller window if a credential leaks.
- No shared secret to rotate across teams.
- Revocation per consumer or in bulk.
Binding to source address and single-use are separate features that dynamic secrets do not provide by themselves.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Never revoked:** Vault still revokes them, and Vault cannot delete copies from client memory.
- ✗ **B. Source address binding:** dynamic credentials are not bound to a network address, unless a different feature is configured.
- ✗ **C. One-read credential:** a dynamic credential can be used repeatedly until its lease ends; one-time use applies to wrapping tokens and SSH one-time passwords.
- ✓ **D. Short window and unique identity (correct):** expiry limits what a leaked value can do and unique users make audits attribute access to one consumer.

## Key idea
Short-lived unique credentials shrink the leak window and make auditing exact.
Q009833:
## Short TTLs and PKI
PKI documentation recommends short TTLs. Revocation is then less needed, so CRLs stay short and the engine scales to large workloads. Each running instance can have its own certificate, avoiding sharing and rollover pain. Certificates can be fetched into memory at start and discarded at shutdown.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Longest TTL:** a long validity increases exposure and makes revocation lists grow if certificates are revoked.
- ✗ **B. One shared certificate:** sharing is what the design avoids, because revoking it affects all instances at once.
- ✓ **C. Short TTLs and unique certificates (correct):** this cuts the need for revocation and keeps lists small, and every instance can be traced.
- ✗ **D. Store on disk:** ephemeral certificates can be held in memory and discarded, with no need to write them to disk.

## Key idea
With PKI, short-lived unique certificates reduce the need for revocation.
Q009834:
## Enabling engines
`vault secrets enable <type>` mounts an engine at its type name by default; `-path` chooses another path. Paths are case-sensitive: `kv/` and `KV/` are two distinct instances.
For KV, the version is an option on the mount: `-version=2` with `kv`, or the type `kv-v2`. With KV v2 the HTTP API path has `data/` and `metadata/` segments after the mount, so policies must use them.
- `vault secrets list` shows the mounts.
- The API equivalent is a `POST` to `sys/mounts/<path>`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Path must be secret:** `secret/` is the dev server default, but any path is allowed.
- ✓ **B. Version 2 at the chosen path (correct):** the option sets the mode and `kv-v2` is the shorthand for the same thing.
- ✗ **C. Version 1:** the version option applies when mounting, and it is not left for later.
- ✗ **D. No data segment:** KV v2 API paths include `data/`, for example `secret-apps/data/<key>`.

## Key idea
Use -path to choose the mount and -version=2 or kv-v2 to enable versioned KV.
Q009835:
## Tuning a mount
`vault secrets tune` changes global configuration for an enabled engine such as default and maximum TTLs. It does not touch the engine's data or path.
Related commands:
- `vault secrets enable` mounts an engine, `list` shows mounts.
- `vault secrets move` changes the path and revokes secrets.
- `vault secrets disable` removes the engine, revokes its secrets and deletes its stored data.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Mount-level tune (correct):** it updates the TTL ceiling used for leases from that mount from now on.
- ✗ **B. Moves the engine:** a move uses `vault secrets move` with a source and destination.
- ✗ **C. Cluster-wide token TTL:** it affects the targeted secrets engine only; auth mounts are tuned with `vault auth tune`.
- ✗ **D. Shortens existing leases:** tuning sets limits for the mount and is not a bulk lease edit.

## Key idea
Tune adjusts mount settings like max lease TTL in place.
Q009836:
## Enable rules
- Default path: the engine's type, such as `aws/`.
- Multiple mounts: with a few exceptions (cubbyhole, identity), an engine type can be enabled at several paths, each isolated.
- Case-sensitive paths.
- Enabling is available in the CLI (`vault secrets enable`), API (`sys/mounts`) and UI (Secrets engines, then enable a new engine).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. UI only:** the CLI (vault secrets enable), the API (a POST to sys/mounts) and the UI can all enable engines.
- ✗ **B. Free path change:** moving an engine revokes its secrets since leases belong to the original path.
- ✗ **C. One path per type:** most types can be mounted several times, for example one database mount per environment.
- ✓ **D. Case-sensitive (correct):** `kv/` and `KV/` are separate instances of the engine.
- ✓ **E. Default type path (correct):** the path equals the type when none is given.

## Key idea
Default path is the type, paths are case-sensitive, and most engines can be mounted repeatedly.
Q009837:
## KV v1 and v2 paths
The `vault kv` commands work against both versions, but the API endpoints differ. With the engine at `secret/`:
- v1: `vault kv get` uses `secret/<key>`.
- v2: `vault kv get` and `put` use `secret/data/<key>`; `list` and `metadata` use `secret/metadata/<key>`; `undelete` uses `secret/undelete/<key>`, `destroy` uses `secret/destroy/<key>`.
The `-mount` flag spares you from typing `data/` on the CLI, but raw API calls and policies need it. The CLI prints the real path as "Secret Path".

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. data path under v1 API prefix (correct):** reading a version 2 secret is a GET on the mount plus `data/` plus the key.
- ✗ **B. sys/mounts:** this path manages mounts and does not read secrets.
- ✗ **C. Without data:** this is the v1 shape and a v2 mount would not find the secret there.
- ✗ **D. metadata path:** that returns key metadata and versions, not the secret's data.

## Key idea
KV v2 reads go to mount/data/key in the API.
Q009838:
## Delete, undelete, destroy
KV v2 keeps versions and uses soft deletes.
- `vault kv delete`: marks versions as deleted; the data is not removed.
- `vault kv undelete -versions=N`: restores them.
- `vault kv destroy -versions=N`: permanently removes the version data.
- `vault kv metadata delete`: removes all versions and metadata of the key.
Policies can restrict who may soft delete, undelete or destroy.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Destroy:** it permanently removes version data and cannot be reversed.
- ✓ **B. Undelete (correct):** a soft delete marks the version, so undelete reverses it. The recovery needs the `-versions` option.
- ✗ **C. Metadata delete:** it permanently removes every version and the metadata, which is the opposite of recovery.
- ✗ **D. Data removed:** soft deletes keep the data so that recovery is possible.

## Key idea
KV v2 delete is soft and undelete reverses it; destroy and metadata delete are permanent.
Q009839:
## Put versus patch
In KV v2, `vault kv put` writes a new version containing only the keys you pass, so any other field is absent from the new version. `vault kv patch` sets or updates keys without overwriting the rest of the data, creating a new version that merges your change. Both write to `secret/data/<key>` in the API; patch uses the HTTP PATCH method.
- `rollback` writes an older version as the newest one.
- `enable-versioning` turns an existing v1 mount into v2.
- Read the result with `vault kv get -mount=secret web-app`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. kv enable-versioning:** it converts a KV mount to version 2 and does not edit a secret.
- ✗ **B. kv put:** it replaces the whole data of the key with only the keys supplied, so region would be missing from the new version.
- ✓ **C. kv patch (correct):** it merges the supplied field into the existing data and creates a new version, so region is preserved.
- ✗ **D. kv rollback:** it restores an earlier version as the new current one and sets no field value.

## Key idea
Use kv patch to change one field and put to replace the whole secret.
Q009840:
## Generic commands use real API paths
`vault kv get` is a KV-aware helper: it knows whether the mount is version 1 or 2 and inserts `data/` for you. `vault read`, `vault write` and `curl` send exactly the path you type.
- v2 data: `secret/data/<key>`.
- v2 key metadata and version list: `secret/metadata/<key>`.
- The `data/` segment sits right after the mount, before the key name.
The `Secret Path` line printed by `vault kv get` shows the real path.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Full API path (correct):** the generic read sends `secret/data/creds` unchanged, which is the endpoint that returns the secret's data and version metadata.
- ✗ **B. Path without data:** the generic command does not rewrite paths, so this addresses a location the version 2 engine does not serve for reading secrets.
- ✗ **C. Metadata path:** it returns versions, timestamps and custom metadata of the key, not the secret values.
- ✗ **D. Segment after key:** `data/` follows the mount name and precedes the key, so this path names a different, nonexistent key.

## Key idea
vault kv get hides data/; vault read and curl need secret/data/<key>.
